doc.title: Wayne Bergeron interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 29, 2020

title: Locking in with drummers and 'laying back'
summary: Bergeron explains how he finds the drummer's feel, objects to 'lay back', and praises Frank Capp and Peter Erskine.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Okay. Well is there a difference, if you’re playing with the Tom Kubis band or Gordon Goodwin or formerly the Juggernaut, the drummer — I mean I’ve been told that the drummer and the lead trumpet player have to be in sync. And I don’t have a question here © Fillius Jazz Archive -21-
except that if you’re just on this date for one gig how long does it take you to figure out where the drummer is at?

Not very long at all. I just answered this question for somebody else the other day. They were asking me about what I — and I try to go to where — because to get the drummer to budge it’s going to be more difficult. You know? So because here’s the beat and here’s the front half of the beat and here’s the back half of the beat. This is all correct. Right? And so some drummers play, you know like when they’re playing quarter notes they go [scats] so that middle note of the shuffle [scats] some drummers play it on the later part of the beat and they go [scats]. Some play it on the other side. They go [scats]. Like Art Blakey kind of does that a lot [scats] which I think swings really hard you know. And that has to move around depending on the tempo of course. And then some play right down the middle. They go [scats]. Right? You hear how those three things sound very different even singing them. Well when you’re playing eighth notes, especially if the tempo is slow, you need to be aware of where the drummer’s feel is. And if it’s going to be later you can tug on the beat more. You don’t want to drag. I don’t like the term “lay back.” I don’t even — I think that word should be eliminated from education. Because laying back means displacing the time. Count Basie’s band didn’t drag. They laid back. They’d go [scats] when it was written [scats] right? They just changed the rhythm so they’d tug on this thing, and it was a thing that [scats] you know? And that was written [scats]. That’s how that’s written. So that’s laying back to me, where they take the time and they put it in another alternative universe for a minute and then it corrects. So I think playing good time within the rules of the beat you can tug on the beat. You can go [scats]. Right? Whatever tune that is, basically blues or whatever tune that is. I’m tugging at the beat but I’m still in time. I’m not going [scats]. I’m not dragging you know. And so kids, when they say to lay back they start dragging. And even if you’re playing a slow swing chart it has to have forward motion even if you’re tugging at the beat, if that makes any senses. So I think that we do kids an injustice by telling them to lay back. No make them play in time. Good time swings really hard. And to quote Andy Martin, who is one of my best friends and also one of my very favorite trombone players on this planet, when somebody starts dragging, his line is “dragging isn’t swinging.” So anyway, that’s what I look for. I just kind of find where the drummer is at and if the drummer plays here I’ll play with them so we’re lined up. Especially if I’m going to come into a situation. Frank Capp was really fun to play with because he had a hard swinging right hand, old school, which I like I think because I was just born thirty years too late probably. But Peter Erskine has that. I love playing with Peter Erskine. Whenever I play with him, we play in Dave Slonaker’s band and we played on several recordings together. And I just know where he’s going to put everything. We’re going to go [scats] I know where that note’s going to © Fillius Jazz Archive -22-
be. On Pat Williams’ record man, we have a bunch of stuff like that. And we always look over and smile. I always look at him and go yeah. We have a little connection you know.

It’s kind of a neat thing. Now sometimes I’m fighting a drummer a little bit — okay I’ll play that here. Or maybe they may hear me doing that and they make adjustments. As the lead trumpet player I’m not in charge of the drummer’s feel you know. I’ve got to kind of play with him or her too.
